newsitem.title: USA: Second breast cancer gene common in Jewish women.
newsitem.headline: Second breast cancer gene common in Jewish women.

text.p: Researchers are finding more evidence that as many as one in 40 Jewish women has a gene linked to breast cancer, but there is no consensus on how to apply the new genetic knowledge, scientists said on Tuesday.
"It's a really tough question," said Sue Richards, a geneticist at Baylor College of Medicine who wrote one of two studies of breast-cancer genetics in Wednesday's edition of Nature Genetics.
The journal's two studies add to the understanding of how frequently one of the two genes -- BRCA1 and BRCA2 -- appear in women of Ashkenazi, or Eastern European, Jewish descent.

Based on what is known about the genes, women with BRCA1 have a very high chance of developing breast cancer -- around 85 percent. BRCA2, while linked to breast and ovarian cancer, does not seem to put women at as high a risk.
"Having a BRCA1 mutation is pretty bad. Having BRCA2 -- there is still a question, how bad is it really?" Richards said in a telephone interview from Houston.

Doctors, cancer researchers, genetic testing companies and medical ethics specialists have been deeply divided over how valuable genetic testing is for these two genes, particularly since no good preventive therapy is known for breast cancer. Some women have preventive double mastectomies, but doctors do not all agree with that drastic step.
BRCA1 seems to occur in about one in 100 Ashkenazi women, and BRCA2 also appears in about one in 100. Overall, about one in 40 of the women have one defect or the other.

"It's hard to come out and say no one should be tested, but they need to think about it ahead of time very seriously," Richards said, adding that in addition to the lack of preventive therapy, there are the risks of the loss of health insurance, job discrimination and psychological damage from the testing.

Tests are available through some commercial outlets. OncorMed Inc. of Gaithersburg, Maryland, announced on Tuesday it was expanding its testing program to all Ashkenazi women identified as being at high risk because of a family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
Previously OncorMed's "Heritage Panel" test was available only to high-risk women who were affected by breast or ovarian cancer or who were related to someone known to have the genetic defect.
